variants.name: ExecutorService.shutdown + awaitTermination
variants.implementation_notes: The JDK's own vocabulary is two-phase: shutdown() initiates an orderly shutdown in which previously submitted tasks run but no new ones are accepted, and awaitTermination() is the completion step - the javadoc says explicitly that shutdown does not wait and names the pattern (first shutdown, then shutdownNow if lingering tasks must be cancelled). Use this form for pools and task-based workers; keep the flag-and-join form below when the participant is a single object with resources the executor cannot release for you.
pitfalls: shutdown() returning does not mean anything has stopped - only isTerminated()/awaitTermination() answer that, and ignoring them lets the JVM exit while tasks still write.
Tasks that swallow InterruptedException (or never block) make shutdownNow useless: interrupt status must be restored (Thread.currentThread().interrupt()) and the task must check it or exit.
Calling shutdown/awaitTermination from one of the pool's own tasks deadlocks (the caller occupies a worker), and awaiting while holding a lock the worker needs deadlocks too.
A shutdown hook that calls awaitTermination without a bound turns JVM exit into a hang; give the second phase a deadline.

variants.name: Worker object with volatile flag, interrupt and join
variants.implementation_notes: For a worker you own (a session, a connection reader, a loop with its own resources) the pattern is hand-written but small: a volatile flag is the latch, shutdown() sets it idempotently, interrupt() (or a sentinel on the queue) wakes the worker out of a blocking call, and join() is phase 2's completion. The interrupt status exists exactly for this - the tutorial stresses that the interrupted thread must support its own interruption - and the cleanup belongs in a finally block so it survives exceptions. Use it when the participant's resources are not managed by an executor.
pitfalls: A non-volatile flag may never be seen by the worker thread: visibility, not just atomicity, is why the field must be volatile (or an atomic).

InterruptedException clears the interrupt status and can arrive at any blocking call: swallowing it makes the worker unstoppable, while running the cleanup inside an interruptible wait lets the second phase be cut short - restore the flag and clean up outside the wait.

Joining the current thread, joining an unstarted thread, or joining while holding the worker's lock all deadlock; so does waiting for a worker that is itself blocked on a resource the controller holds.
deamon-ness is not a shutdown protocol: a daemon thread is stopped abruptly at JVM exit with no cleanup at all.
